issues.item: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, a trigger based on being in a similar natural environment is hard to reconcile unless the robbery specifically occurred in wilderness or outdoors; nothing else in the profile supports that context, making this trigger clinically incongruent with the rest of the presentation.

Helicopter/aircraft sounds are not a plausible trauma-linked trigger for a mugging/robbery in the absence of any supporting memory or threat content suggesting emergency-response, combat, or disaster context. This appears disconnected from the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to link clinically unless the robbery specifically involved aircraft or a major police response; this trigger is not supported by the other selected items and feels trauma-incongruent.

Alcohol smell could occur if the perpetrator had been drinking, but that link is not reflected anywhere else in the profile, so as selected it appears weakly grounded in the trauma narrative compared with the other more plausible interpersonal-danger cues.

issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma in a 67-year-old male, contamination and body-focused shame are hard to reconcile unless there was a sexual assault or severe bodily violation component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. These appraisals fit poorly with the stated trauma type and with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Burnt smell is a highly specific trigger that suggests fire, smoke, or explosion exposure. In a robbery/mugging profile it lacks support from the threat and appraisal items and does not connect plausibly to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery in a 67-year-old male, 'body shame' is hard to reconcile unless there was prominent sexual assault, disfigurement, or injury-focused trauma content, which is not reflected elsewhere in threat, memory, or strategies. It reads as a qualitatively different appraisal from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery victim, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the report centers on external danger and mistrust (suspicious people, loud noises, hypervigilance, alarm when touched, mistrust, humiliation), but this item implies morally dissonant behaviour by the patient during the event. That is possible, but without any supporting memory or strategy content it stands apart from the otherwise victimization-focused formulation and is harder to reconcile clinically than the other items. The remaining items are broadly coherent with robbery trauma and with the active formulation path Negative Appraisals → Threat and Threat → Triggers.

vignette:
Richard is a 67-year-old hotel manager who came to treatment more than a year after being robbed on his way home from work. He had closed out a late shift and stopped in the hotel parking structure to check a service door he thought had been left unsecured. The garage was half lit, echoing with distant traffic and the sharp slam of a car door. A man stepped out from between two concrete pillars, close enough that Richard caught the stale smell of alcohol before he fully understood what was happening. When Richard hesitated, the man shoved him hard, demanded his wallet and watch, and cursed at him for moving too slowly. What stayed with Richard was not only the fear of being hurt but the feeling of being overpowered and exposed, an older man in a suit and name badge, handled like he was defenseless. By the time the police arrived, he was shaken less by the loss of money than by the sense that something basic had been stripped from him.

In the weeks that followed, Richard found himself turning the robbery into a verdict about people and about himself. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, especially strangers whose intentions were not immediately clear. The attack also settled into him as a humiliation he could not shake; he replayed how he had frozen, how easily the man had pushed him aside, and felt permanently diminished by it. Alongside that was a broader conviction that the world was simply dangerous now, not unpredictably so but fundamentally so, as if safety had been revealed as a naïve assumption he should never have made. Living with those beliefs kept his body in a state of readiness. He was superalert wherever he went, scanning faces, doorways, and hands, and he remained on guard even inside his own home, checking locks repeatedly and listening for sounds outside at night. If his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly while he was washing dishes or reading, he reacted with an immediate jolt of alarm before he could recognize her.

That constant state of watchfulness made the world feel full of signals he needed to catch before something bad happened again. At the hotel, where he spends his days moving between the lobby, bar area, elevators, and loading entrances, he notices people other staff might dismiss as ordinary: a guest lingering too long without checking in, someone pacing near the front desk, a man in wrinkled clothes watching employees change shifts. People acting suspiciously pull his attention instantly and completely. He finds himself tracking where they are standing, how close they are, whether their hands are visible. Loud noises hit him the same way. A tray crashing in the banquet hall, a door slamming in the service corridor, even a burst of laughter from the bar can make his body surge before he has time to think. The smell of alcohol is especially potent. When a guest leans in at reception with liquor on his breath, Richard is abruptly back in the parking structure, his chest tight, his mind narrowing around danger.

Over time, these moments have not stayed confined to the places that would objectively remind someone of a robbery. Because he is already braced for threat, the triggers seem to appear everywhere. At home he watches men walking slowly past the house and feels the same suspicion gather in him. In restaurants he chooses seats facing the entrance and stiffens if he hears shouting or glasses breaking. He has become careful about moving through his own hotel after dark, sometimes asking a younger employee to accompany him to the garage under the pretense of checking maintenance issues. He does not describe this as fear so much as common sense; to Richard, staying on guard is what a person does once he has learned what people are capable of.

His wife has told him he is harder now, quicker to assume the worst about strangers and less able to relax even during ordinary evenings at home. Richard hears that and feels both defensive and ashamed. The humiliation of the robbery remains raw for him, and what frightens him most is not just that another attack could happen, but that he has become someone who is always waiting for it. He sought help after startling violently when a bellman touched his arm from behind in the hotel lobby, causing a scene in front of guests and leaving him shaken for hours. He says he wants to stop living as if every suspicious glance, every loud sound, every trace of alcohol means he is about to be cornered again, but he is afraid that lowering his guard would be the same as making the mistake that got him robbed in the first place.
